entries.claim: The Transistor API uses API keys to authenticate all requests, sent via an HTTP header named x-api-key
entries.verbatim: The Transistor API uses API keys to authenticate all requests. Your API keys can be viewed and reset in the [Account Area](https://dashboard.transistor.fm/account) of your Transistor Dashboard. Each API request must include an HTTP header `x-api-key` with its value being your API key.

entries.claim: API requests are rate-limited to 10 requests per 10 seconds; exceeding this returns a 429 HTTP error code and blocks access for 10 seconds
entries.verbatim: API requests are rate-limited to 10 requests per 10 seconds. If this limit is exceeded, you will be receive a `429` HTTP error code, and access will be blocked for 10 seconds.

entries.claim: The Transistor API is built around the JSON:API specification
entries.verbatim: The Transistor API is built around the [JSON:API](https://jsonapi.org) specification.

entries.claim: The API supports sparse fieldsets, letting a request specify only particular fields to return, e.g. fields[episode][]=title&fields[episode][]=media_url
entries.verbatim: Let's say you want to retrieve an Episode but only return the title and media\_url. In your request you can specify `fields[episode][]=title&fields[episode][]=media_url`.

entries.claim: The API supports including a resource's related resources in one request, e.g. include[]=show, and this can be combined with sparse fieldsets
entries.verbatim: You can also return a resource's related resources in one single API request instead of multiuple requests. For example, you may want to retrieve an Episode, but also include its parent Show resource. In your request you can specify `include[]=show`.

exemplars: Since his launch, he's already hit #1 on the Apple Podcasts' Education charts:

A public podcast has one RSS feed that you share as widely as possible. A private podcast works differently: every subscriber gets their own unique RSS feed, so you control exactly who can listen and can see what each person listens to.

You make the podcast. Transistor takes care of getting it out into the world. Upload your finished audio or video, add a title and show notes, then publish right away or schedule your episode for later.
